title: Washing Your Face: The Step This Journal Has Been Assuming

article.lede: Ten pieces in this journal open by telling you to start with a gentle cleanser. Not one of them says what gentle means. And the six-step protocol we describe elsewhere contains no cleanser at all, which makes the omission slightly worse than careless. So: this is the article about washing your face. It is mostly about what washing does not do, and about the one question that genuinely has two answers.
article.meta_description: Cleansing is the step this journal kept assuming. What a wash is actually for, why the evening one matters most, and how to decide about mornings.

sections.heading: The step we kept assuming
paragraphs: We went back through the archive to check. The phrase "start with a gentle cleanser" opens ten articles here, where it functions as an establishing shot — the sentence you write to get to the interesting part. Meanwhile the six formulations we sequence into a protocol begin at exfoliation. There is no wash in it. That is not a gap in the writing so much as a gap in the thinking.

It happens for a dull reason. Cleansing is the least commercially interesting step in skincare. Nobody builds a house on it, and it is difficult to say anything about a rinse-off product that sounds like news. So it becomes throat-clearing before the actives arrive.

The awkward part is that for most people the wash is the step with the most room to go wrong. A serum that underperforms costs you an outcome you were never certain of. A wash that strips the skin every night and every morning makes everything applied afterwards feel worse, and it does so quietly, over months, while you blame the serum.

sections.heading: What a wash is actually for
paragraphs: Three things come off a face. Sunscreen. Sebum, along with whatever it has picked up and whatever it has turned into over the course of a day. And the ordinary deposits of being out in the world — road particulate, cooking grease, dust, whatever your hands transferred. That is the list. It is shorter than the category implies.

What a wash is not for is deep cleaning, because there is no depth available to it. The outer layer of skin is a barrier whose entire function is to keep things out, and nothing you apply to the surface crosses it in any quantity worth discussing. A cleanser sits on the top few micrometres for forty seconds and then goes down the sink. It does not detoxify anything. Pores do not open in warm water and close in cold — they have no muscle to do it with. What changes is how soft the sebum inside them has become, which is useful, and which is not the same claim at all.

This is a relief rather than a disappointment. It means washing is a small mechanical task with a low ceiling. You can do it well; you cannot do it brilliantly. There is no cleanser that will change your face. There are cleansers that leave the skin in a better state to be worked on than others, and that is the whole of the competition.

sections.heading: The evening wash, which is close to non-negotiable
paragraphs: If you wear sunscreen daily — and this journal takes the position that you should — the evening wash follows from it. Modern SPF films are engineered to stay on through heat, sweat and swimming. That resistance is the point of them, and it is also the reason water alone will not take one off. You need a surfactant, which is to say you need a cleanser, which is why the evening question closes itself.

Sebum makes the second half of the argument. It is mostly triglycerides, wax esters and squalene, and squalene oxidises readily on a warm surface in daylight, so the film on your face at eight in the evening is not chemically what your skin secreted at eight in the morning. Sleeping in it is not a catastrophe. It is untidy, and it sits between your skin and whatever comes next — the order in which everything else goes on quietly assumes a clean, slightly damp surface underneath.

The technique is not complicated enough to justify a section, so here it is in a sentence. Lukewarm water, a cleanser that suits you, thirty to sixty seconds, rinse until the skin stops feeling slippery, then pat dry rather than rub. That is the entire method. It has been sold to you at considerably greater length.

sections.heading: The morning is a real question
paragraphs: Overnight, your face meets a pillowcase and its own oil. That is the whole exposure. If you washed properly the night before, there is a perfectly good argument that you wake up with a clean face, and that washing it again removes lipids the skin spent hours rebuilding, in exchange for nothing.

There is an equally good argument on the other side, and it is not weaker. Some people produce a great deal of sebum overnight. Some apply a rich night cream or a balm that is still sitting there at seven in the morning. Some sleep warm, or sleep in a warm climate, and wake up damp. Some are about to apply a sunscreen that will sit badly on top of last night's residue and pill by ten. For all of them the morning wash is preparation rather than habit. The two ends of the day have different jobs, and the morning's job is to get the skin ready to be protected.
The honest position is that this question has a personal answer, and that anybody handing you a universal rule is handing you their own skin's answer with the labelling removed.

sections.heading: A way to decide instead of a rule to obey
paragraphs: Try it as a test rather than a belief. For one week, in the mornings, rinse with lukewarm water and your hands and nothing else, then continue with the rest of your routine exactly as before. Same products, same order, same evening wash. One variable, one week: long enough for a pattern to show, short enough that you will finish it.

Then ask what you noticed. Does the skin feel coated by mid-morning, or does it feel like skin? Does sunscreen go on evenly, or does it slide and pill where it did not before? And the thing people forget to check: how does the face look at six in the evening, when any difference in oil will have declared itself.

Comfortable skin, sunscreen sitting flat, nothing worse at the end of the day — you did not need the morning wash, and you can stop. Shine by nine, pilling, a rougher-looking surface — you do, and that is settled too. Neither answer makes you more or less serious about your skin. It is sebum, and sebum varies enormously between people, and between seasons.

One caveat worth stating plainly. If your skin already feels tight and squeaky after washing, do not run this experiment yet. That tightness means the wash you own is taking more than it needs to, and until you fix the product, changing the frequency only changes how often the problem happens.

sections.heading: Double cleansing, kept in proportion
paragraphs: The practice is straightforward and the chemistry behind it is sound. An oil or balm goes on first and dissolves the oil-soluble things — sunscreen, long-wear makeup, sebum — because like dissolves like. A water-based wash follows and carries away the oil along with everything now suspended in it. It came out of routines where people wore substantial sunscreen and substantial makeup every day, and in that context it does something a single mild gel often cannot.

So the question is not whether double cleansing works. It is whether you are the person it was designed for. If you wear a high-SPF film daily, or long-wear base, or both, one pass frequently leaves residue — you can verify this yourself with a cotton pad after your usual wash, which is a more useful piece of evidence than anything we could tell you.

If you wear nothing but your own sebum, two washes is one wash too many, and the second is where the tightness comes from. Double cleansing is a technique matched to a load, not a level of commitment. Nobody is grading you on it.

sections.heading: What gentle means, and why we can afford to say
paragraphs: Since we have used the word ten times without defining it: gentle is mostly a question of the surfactant system, the part of the formula doing the actual work and rarely the part named on the front of the bottle. Milder blends behave better than the harsher sulphates common in older formulations. Foam is not evidence of cleaning; it is evidence of foaming agents, and the two are only loosely related. A wash formulated near the skin's own mildly acidic surface is easier on it than a strongly alkaline bar. The rest of the test is subjective and reliable: after rinsing and patting dry, your face should feel unremarkable. Not tight, not squeaky, not still coated.

Water is the variable nobody mentions. The same cleanser genuinely behaves differently in two cities, because the mineral content of what comes out of your tap changes how surfactants rinse and what they leave behind. If a product that suited you for years turned harsh after you moved, that is a plausible explanation and worth testing before you blame your skin.

One boundary, stated once. Skin that is persistently sore, inflamed or breaking out in a way that affects how you live is not a cleansing problem, and no wash is the answer to it. Those are matters for a doctor, and choosing a different face wash while waiting for an appointment is a way of doing something rather than a way of treating anything.

Now the disclosure that makes this article possible. Zero Lines does not make a cleanser. There are six formulations and none of them is a wash, and there is no plan to attach one to the end of this piece. So we have nothing to steer you towards, and can say the useful thing instead: keep the cleanser you have if it leaves your face comfortable, and replace it with the mildest inexpensive one at your pharmacy if it does not. That is what those ten articles should have said. Start with a wash that leaves your skin feeling like nothing much happened, then get on with the parts worth arguing about.

sources: That the intact outer layer of skin acts as a barrier is among the least controversial ideas in dermatology. The general understanding is that molecules much above a few hundred daltons do not cross it in meaningful amounts, which is why nothing rinsed off the surface can reach anything beneath it.

It is well established in cosmetic science that surfactants remove skin lipids along with oil and soil, that harsher ones remove more, and that water loss through the skin rises temporarily after washing before recovering.

Healthy skin surface is generally understood to be mildly acidic, usually described as sitting somewhere between pH 4.5 and 5.5. Alkaline washing raises it temporarily, with recovery normally measured in hours.
The broad composition of sebum — triglycerides, wax esters and squalene — and the readiness with which squalene oxidises on the skin surface are both long-standing findings rather than recent ones.

title: Dry Skin or Dehydrated Skin? How to Tell Which You Have

article.meta_description: Dry skin is short of lipids; dehydrated skin is short of water. The tells that separate them, why the pinch test fails, and what to reach for next.
article.lede: Two faces can look equally parched and need opposite things. One is short of oil. The other is short of water, and it may well be the shinier of the two. The distinction gets used loosely enough in marketing that it has started to sound invented, which is a shame, because the thing underneath it is real, and it decides whether the next product you buy does anything at all.

sections.heading: The difference is what is missing
paragraphs: Dry skin is a shortage of lipids. The outer layer of skin is usually described as bricks and mortar: flattened cells held together by a fatty matrix of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids, with sebum sitting over the top. Some faces simply produce less of that material. Less mortar, a leakier wall, more water escaping into the air all day. That tendency is largely constitutional, and it is a good part of what people are actually describing when they talk about their skin type.

Dehydrated skin is a shortage of water in that same outer layer. It has nothing to do with what your skin produces. It is about what has been lost recently and not replaced, or what has been pulled out by dry air, heat, wind, aircraft cabins, long hot showers, a cleanser that strips more than it needs to, an exfoliating acid used with more enthusiasm than the skin had asked for.

So one is a supply problem and the other is a balance problem. This is why the same face can be oily and dehydrated at once with no contradiction at all. It is also why the two look so similar from a metre away — dull, tight, fine lines more legible than usual — and why a great many people spend a season treating the wrong one.

sections.heading: One is a trait, the other is a week
paragraphs: The most useful question is not what your skin looks like this morning. It is how long it has looked that way.

Dry skin is settled. It is how your face has behaved for years. Winter makes it worse and a humid August makes it easier, but it does not leave, and you have probably known about it since your twenties. Dehydration has a start date. You can usually name the week: three flights, a hotel with aggressive heating, a new foaming cleanser, a fortnight of retinoid enthusiasm, a holiday spent moving between sun and air conditioning.

Look back three months. If tight and faintly flaky is your baseline, you are dry. If you can point to roughly when it began, you are dehydrated. If you are dry and something recent has made it worse, you are both — which is the most common answer and, as it happens, the easiest to act on.

One complication is worth knowing. Sebum output tends to fall gradually across the decades, so someone who was oily and occasionally dehydrated at twenty-five can be genuinely dry at fifty-five. The answer you settled on ten years ago may have quietly expired. That drift belongs to the longer arc of how skin changes with age, and it is slow enough that most people miss the handover entirely.

sections.heading: The tell that catches people out
paragraphs: Here is the counter-intuitive one. Dehydrated skin often reads as oilier, not drier.

The pattern is easy to recognise once you have seen it: tight and faintly uncomfortable in the morning, unmistakably shiny by four in the afternoon, and still tight underneath the shine. People with this combination usually conclude they are oily, buy something more astringent, and make it worse. The common explanation is that skin increases sebum to compensate for a surface that is losing water too quickly. That is plausible and widely repeated. The honest limit of it is that the pattern is far easier to observe than the mechanism is to demonstrate in any particular face.

The visual tells repay learning. Fine, crepey lines across the cheeks or under the eyes that were not there last month, and that soften when you press a damp fingertip to them. Makeup that separates or clings by mid-morning. A brief sting when a serum goes on that never used to sting. And pores that look larger than they did — not because pores open and close, which they do not, but because skin holding less water sits less taut around each opening, so the opening reads bigger.

Genuinely dry skin looks different at close range. It is matte all day, faintly rough or dusty in texture, and it sheds in fine powdery scale rather than in patches. It rarely turns shiny at all, in any weather, at any hour.

sections.heading: Why the pinch test tells you almost nothing
paragraphs: The pinch test turns up in nearly every article on this subject. Pinch the skin, usually on the back of the hand, watch how quickly the tent collapses. Slow means dehydrated. It is repeated with such confidence that it sounds like established practice.

It is established practice — for a different question. Skin turgor is a rough clinical sign of whole-body fluid loss, used by clinicians alongside several other observations, and it is blunt even there. What it registers is the behaviour of the whole tissue: dermis, elastin, subcutaneous fat, total body water. Cosmetic dehydration is a matter of the outermost layer, a few dozen micrometres deep. A pinch cannot feel a layer that thin.

On the face it is worse than unhelpful. Facial skin is thinner and more mobile, and elastic recoil slows with age regardless of how well hydrated anyone is. A well-hydrated sixty-year-old will fail the test. A badly dehydrated twenty-five-year-old will pass it comfortably. It reads age far more reliably than it reads water, which makes it, at best, a confusing input to a decision you are trying to get right.
Your own observations across a week — shine, tightness, how makeup sits, whether fine lines come and go — will tell you considerably more than any single manoeuvre performed once.

sections.heading: Humectant or lipid
paragraphs: This is the practical payoff, and it comes down to two categories of ingredient.

Humectants bind water and hold it in the surface layer: glycerin, hyaluronic acid, urea, panthenol, sodium PCA, various sugars. They are what dehydrated skin is short of. Lipids and occlusives supply the fatty material that keeps water from leaving: squalane, shea butter, ceramides, cholesterol, plant oils, petrolatum at the heavier end. They are what dry skin is short of.

If you are dehydrated, lead with a humectant, and put something over it. A humectant left bare on the face in genuinely dry air can draw water from the deeper layers up to the surface, where it evaporates, which is the mechanism behind hyaluronic acid feeling worse in dry air than in humid air. The humectant is not the problem. Leaving it uncovered is.

If you are dry, lead with lipids. A humectant on lipid-poor skin is water poured into a leaking container: you will feel the difference for an hour and lose it by lunch. And if you are both, the order is humectant onto damp skin, lipid on top. Nothing more complicated than that.

sections.heading: What to take away first
paragraphs: Before you add anything, look hard at what is already in the routine. Subtraction tends to move things faster than addition, and it costs nothing.

The usual suspects: a cleanser that leaves the face squeaky, which is the sensation of stripped lipids rather than of cleanliness; water hot enough to be enjoyable; exfoliating acids more than twice a week; two or three actives layered together because each was recommended on its own by someone who did not know about the others. Any of these can produce a face that looks dry while being nothing of the kind.

This is where the honest limit sits. For a fair number of people the answer is not a new product at all — it is a gentler cleanser and less frequent acid, and the face settles by itself in a fortnight. That is an unhelpful thing for a skincare house to say, and it happens to be true. We have nothing on sale yet, so there is nothing here we are steering you towards.

sections.heading: How to know within a fortnight whether you chose right
paragraphs: Change one thing. Not three. If you have decided you are dehydrated, add a humectant serum under whatever you already use and cover it. If you have decided you are dry, add a lipid-rich cream at night. Leave everything else alone and give it two weeks — long enough for the surface layer to turn over more or less completely, short enough that you can still remember where you started.

If you chose right, the reading is reasonably clear. Dehydrated skin given water and a lid tends to respond within days: the afternoon shine settles, the tightness beneath it goes, fine lines look softer in the mirror by the end of the first week. Dry skin given lipids moves more slowly and more steadily — less roughness, less flaking, comfort that holds through the day rather than for the hour after application.

If you chose wrong, that is legible too. A humectant on genuinely dry skin gives a pleasant hour and then nothing, and can feel faintly tacky by evening. A rich cream on skin that was only dehydrated feels heavy, pills under makeup, and does not settle the shine, because water was never what you were adding. Neither outcome is a setback of any consequence. Swap categories and run the fortnight again.

Two cautions. Do not run this experiment against drinking more water and expect to learn much: correcting a genuine shortfall in fluid intake does show on the face, while going from adequate to abundant largely does not, which is the narrower true thing about water intake and skin. And if skin is cracked, persistently itchy, or inflamed in a way that will not settle, none of the above applies. That is a question for a doctor, not for a moisturiser.

sources: The outer layer of skin is generally understood as a brick-and-mortar structure: flattened corneocytes set in a matrix of ceramides, cholesterol and free fatty acids, which together limit how quickly water leaves the skin.
Transepidermal water loss is a long-established measurement in skin research, and it is generally understood to rise when that lipid matrix is depleted, disrupted or stripped by surfactants.

Skin holds its own humectant system, commonly called natural moisturising factor — a mixture of amino acids, urea, lactate and salts inside the surface cells — and its levels are generally understood to vary with season, humidity and washing.

It is generally understood that humectants draw water both from deeper in the skin and from the surrounding air, so ambient humidity changes how they behave, and that occlusive or emollient materials slow the loss of that water to the atmosphere.

title: Where the Money Goes in a Jar of Cream

article.lede: We have nothing to sell you. Six formulations exist, none of them on sale, no ingredient list published, no date in the diary. That makes this a strange moment to write about price, and the only honest one. Once there is a jar with a number on it, everything a house says about cost reads as justification. So here is where the money in a jar of cream goes, ours included, before we have a jar.
article.meta_description: Glass, short filling runs, safety work, market-by-market paperwork and retail margin: a pre-launch house itemises where the money in a jar of cream goes.

sections.heading: Why this can only be written now
paragraphs: A brand explaining its costs while its product sits on a shelf is doing something close to special pleading, even when every number it gives you is true. The explanation arrives attached to an invitation to pay. You can hear the tilt in it. We will not be immune to that later, which is the reason for writing it down while we still have nothing at stake.

The question people actually type is "why is skincare so expensive", and it usually contains two questions wearing one coat. The first is whether the price is arbitrary. The second is whether the expensive one is better. They have different answers, and the honest answer to the second is less satisfying than either side would like.
So: an itemised walk through the stack, in roughly the order the money leaves. Some of these lines are larger than most people expect. One of them is much smaller.

sections.heading: The jar usually costs more than the cream
paragraphs: Pick up a jar of moisturiser and weigh it. The heft is deliberate, and it is not free. A thick-walled glass jar, a weighted cap, an inner sealing disc, a shrink band, a folding carton, a leaflet printed in six languages, sometimes a sheet of tissue. Decoration is a separate step again: hot foil, screen printing, embossing, each done on different machinery, often in a different factory, each with its own minimum order.

Some of that weight is theatre. Some of it is doing a job. A formula that oxidises in daylight wants an opaque airless pump, which costs several times what a screw-top jar costs, and the decision is really about how long a formula stays the thing it says it is. The uncomfortable part is that you usually cannot tell which case you are looking at. Heavy glass reads as serious. It is also the cheapest way to make a cheap formula feel expensive.

Then the filling. A run of two thousand units and a run of two hundred thousand need the same line changeover, the same clean-down before and after, the same first-article checks, roughly the same operator hours. Those costs land on the batch, then get divided by the units in it. Small batches carry them badly. Components make it worse: minimum orders mean buying ten thousand caps to fill three thousand jars, and the remainder sits in a warehouse costing rent until it is either used or written off.
All of this happens after the formula is finished. The years of benchwork behind a formulation are their own cost, spent whether the product sells well, badly, or not at all.

sections.heading: Safety and stability, the work nobody sees
paragraphs: Before a cosmetic can be sold in the EU or the UK it needs a safety assessment signed by a qualified assessor, and a file behind it holding the toxicological profile of every raw material, the exposure calculations, the manufacturing detail. This is not a form you tick. The assessor asks for data, sends things back, and charges for the work. Change a supplier, a preservative or a fragrance component and a good part of it is done again.

Stability testing is slower and stranger. Filled packs go into ovens at several temperatures and sit there for months, alongside freeze-thaw cycles and light exposure, and are pulled at intervals to be checked for pH drift, viscosity, colour, smell, separation. The pack is tested with the formula in it, because glass, plastic and the formula all interact. Preservative systems are checked by deliberately introducing micro-organisms and counting what happens to them over weeks. Real time takes real time. There is no way to buy your way past twelve weeks.

Human tolerance work sits on top of that, and it is worth being precise about what it does and does not establish. The phrase "dermatologically tested" covers an enormous range of effort, from a small supervised patch test to something considerably more thorough, and it promises far less than the confidence with which it is printed. It is a real cost. It is not the same as a claim about what the product does.

sections.heading: The same paperwork, market after market
paragraphs: A product notified in the EU is not thereby notified in the UK, and neither notification helps anywhere else. Each territory wants its own submission, and in most cases a named party legally responsible for the product inside that territory. Labels have to carry the required languages. Any claim printed on the carton needs evidence held on file, per claim, per market.

Our own shops make this concrete in a way we did not fully appreciate at the start. Gibraltar, Andorra and Marbella: one of those three sits inside the EU and two of them do not. One has no VAT at all, another has its own, considerably lower. The same jar moving from one of our shops to another is, on paper, an export, with the customs formalities that implies. Three shops, three sets of rules, one product.

None of this is expensive in the way a machine is expensive. It is expensive in the way that doing the same careful thing four times is expensive: translation, a re-plated carton, another responsible person, another dossier. It falls hardest on small houses and small markets, which is part of why a niche product costs what it does, and part of why some products simply never appear in your country at all.

sections.heading: What the shop takes
paragraphs: Then distribution, which is where the largest single multiple usually sits. In beauty, the step from what a brand receives to what you pay is commonly around a doubling, and can be more. That is not a scandal on its own. The shop pays rent on a street worth being on, employs and trains people who will stand there all day, holds stock it has paid for, funds the samples in your bag, and takes back what comes back.

Selling direct online moves the money rather than removing it. Acquiring a customer through paid channels can cost as much as a retailer's margin would have. Add payment processing, warehousing, packing for transit, the parcels that arrive broken, and a customer service function that has to exist. Brands that pass their whole retail saving to the customer are rarer than the marketing around direct-to-consumer suggests.

One more line that nobody itemises: discounting. If a house expects a meaningful share of its stock to sell at a promotional price, the full price has to be set high enough to survive that. A product that is permanently on offer has a price designed to be discounted. It is worth noticing which prices in your bathroom are real prices.

sections.heading: The actives are rarely the expensive part
paragraphs: Here is the line that lands badly, and it holds at every price point, including whichever one we end up at. The raw materials are usually the smallest meaningful cost in the jar. Actives are used at fractions of a per cent; even a genuinely costly peptide, bought by the kilogramme, works out to small change per unit. The bulk of the formula is water, humectants, emulsifiers, thickeners, preservative. Priced by weight, that base is cheap.

There are exceptions and they are mostly unglamorous. A generous load of a good oil costs real money. So do low-yield botanical extracts, awkward supply chains, and the plain logistics of moving liquid: bringing mineral water down from a Pyrenean spring to a laboratory in Barcelona costs more than taking it from the mains, for reasons that have nothing to do with romance. Whether that difference is one you could see in a mirror is a separate question, and one we would rather leave open than answer flatteringly.

It follows that cost tells you almost nothing about formulation. Neither, quite, does the label. An ingredient list gives you descending order down to one per cent and then stops being informative, and it says nothing at all about grade, purity, or whether the formula was built around its active or simply had it dropped in near the end. Both signals available to you, price and position on a list, are weaker than they look.

sections.heading: A better question than whether it is worth it
paragraphs: This leaves two comfortable positions, and both are wrong. The first says expensive skincare is a con, the same emulsion in better glass. Sometimes it is. Often somebody did pay for the stability work, the better vessel, a base designed around what it carries rather than around cost per litre. The second says you get what you pay for, which is wrong at least as often, and in a more expensive direction.

Price predicts packaging, distribution and marketing spend fairly well. It predicts formulation quality badly, in both directions. Large manufacturers have volume, in-house laboratories and serious testing budgets, which is exactly why some inexpensive products are properly made. And a high price can be paid entirely to the rent on a good street. Neither fact tells you anything about the jar in your hand.

So the question worth carrying into a shop is not "is this worth it", which cannot be answered without knowing what you value. It is narrower: what specifically am I paying for here. Is the packaging protecting the formula or performing seriousness? Is the claim on the carton narrow enough to be checkable, or broad enough to be unfalsifiable? Is this a real price or a discount waiting to happen?

When we price ours, every force described above will be acting on us, and you should put the same question to us that we have just handed you. Some of what you would be paying for will be work you cannot see and might reasonably value. Some of it will be a shop in Marbella with rent to pay. We would rather you knew which was which.

sources: Cosmetic products sold in the EU and the UK must have a safety assessment completed by a qualified assessor, and a product information file held for them, before they go on sale. This is a matter of public regulation rather than industry custom.

Ingredient lists are given in descending order of concentration down to one per cent, below which ingredients may be listed in any order. This is a long-standing labelling convention, not a research finding.

Preservative systems are generally checked by deliberately introducing micro-organisms into a finished formula and measuring how the population falls over a period of weeks. The approach is standard across the industry.

It is generally understood within the cosmetics trade that raw materials account for a small share of a finished product's retail price, and that most cosmetic actives are used at fractions of a per cent of a formula.

title: Why Your Face Feels Tight After Washing

article.lede: There is a particular feeling after washing your face. The skin across the cheekbones draws in. Smiling takes a fraction more effort than it did a minute ago. Most people read this as the cleanser having worked, and reach for a moisturiser to settle it down. It is worth sitting with a less flattering possibility: that the tightness is not evidence of clean skin at all, only evidence of what the cleanser took with it on the way out.
article.meta_description: Tightness after washing is something the cleanser produces, not proof of clean skin. Why the feeling persuades, and a one-week test that costs nothing.

sections.heading: What the tightness actually is
paragraphs: The sensation is mechanical before it is anything else. Cleansing is done by surfactants, molecules with a water-loving end and an oil-loving end, which is what allows oil to leave your face in water that would otherwise refuse to carry it. They are effective. They are also not selective. They lift the day's sebum, sunscreen and city grime, and on the same pass they take a share of the lipids sitting between the cells of the outermost layer, and some of the small water-binding compounds held inside those cells.

What remains is a surface that holds water less well than it did ten minutes earlier. As it dries it contracts slightly, the way most thin materials do when they lose moisture, and because it is anchored to living tissue underneath it cannot contract freely. That restrained shrinkage is roughly what you are feeling. A physical event, occurring in the top fraction of a millimetre of you.

Which is also why it passes. Give it an hour and the feeling usually goes, as water moves up from the tissue below and the surface rehydrates itself. The sensation is real. It is simply a transient state of the outermost layer, and reading it as a verdict on how clean your face is confuses one thing for another entirely.

sections.heading: The pH your face is left at
paragraphs: Skin's surface sits on the acid side of neutral, generally around pH 4.5 to 5.5. Traditional soap is strongly alkaline, and that is a consequence of how soap is made rather than a failing of any particular bar. Wash with it and the surface is pushed several points up the scale in the space of thirty seconds.

Skin brings itself back down on its own, over a few hours. But a good deal of the quiet housekeeping the surface does is tuned to that acidic range: the enzyme activity that lets spent cells detach in an orderly way, the processing of lipids into their organised arrangement. Push the pH up twice a day, every day, and the housekeeping is done in less favourable conditions than it was designed for.

The honest limit of this is that most of it has been characterised under laboratory conditions, and how much any individual face notices it varies enormously. Some people wash with a hard alkaline soap for forty years and are perfectly comfortable. Nobody can tell you which you are from a distance, including us. What can be said plainly is that a cleanser leaving you tight is a cleanser that has changed the state of your skin surface, and the tightness is the receipt.

sections.heading: Why the feeling is so convincing
paragraphs: We learned the squeak somewhere else. A plate that squeaks under a finger is clean, a strand of hair that squeaks is clean, and the association transfers to the face without anyone consciously deciding it should. The squeak is friction between two surfaces stripped of the film that was lubricating them. On a dinner plate that is exactly what you want.

Then there is the timing, which is the more interesting part. Skincare gives feedback on a scale of weeks, sometimes months, mostly in the form of you failing to notice anything and wondering whether you have wasted your money. A cleanser answers in eight seconds. It arrives with a physical sensation at precisely the moment you are looking for confirmation that the thing you just did was worth doing.

Immediate bodily sensations are far more persuasive than their information content justifies, and the industry has known this for a very long time. Foam volume, the cooling sting, the tingle, the squeak: these are sensory cues, they are inexpensive to formulate for, and they run more or less independently of whether a product suits your face. None of this makes a single tight evening harmful. It does mean the feeling is not telling you what you think it is telling you.

sections.heading: The moisturiser is often solving the cleanser
paragraphs: Watch the sequence. Skin goes tight. A cream goes on. Within half a minute the tightness is gone and the cream has demonstrated its worth. What the relief actually measures, though, is the size of the deficit that opened up two minutes earlier, at the sink.

This is why the question of what order to apply things in so often gets asked from the wrong end. People add a step, then another step, to close a gap that a different first step would not have opened. The routine grows. Each addition feels justified, because each one produces a noticeable improvement on the state the previous product left behind.

A cleanser that leaves the face comfortable changes what everything after it is for. The serum is no longer partly a repair job. The moisturiser is a choice rather than an obligation. And you find out what the rest of your routine is actually doing, which is information you cannot get while it is busy compensating.

sections.heading: A test you can run this week without buying anything
paragraphs: Wash your face at night exactly as you always do. Same product, same water temperature, same length of time. Pat dry rather than rub. Then apply nothing at all, and set a timer for ten minutes.

At ten minutes, pay attention. Not for a verdict, just for a description. Is the skin comfortable and unremarkable, the way the back of your forearm is unremarkable? Or is it drawn tight across the cheekbones, faintly itchy, papery around the mouth, stinging a little at the sides of the nose? There is no scoring system. You will know which one it is.

Run it five nights before you conclude anything, because one night is an anecdote. Sleep, a flight, a change in the weather and a hot shower all move the result. Skip the test on a night you have exfoliated, since the difference between exfoliating weekly and exfoliating daily shows up as tightness of its own and will confound the reading. Skip it after a razor pass too, for the same reason. If you are also weighing up whether to cleanse twice a day or once, hold that question until this one has an answer, or you will change two variables at once and learn nothing from either.

One caveat, and it matters. If the ten minutes is genuinely uncomfortable, if anything burns or stings properly, stop and put your moisturiser on. The test is not worth enduring. The answer in that case has already arrived.

sections.heading: What to read on the label if it fails
paragraphs: Ingredients appear in descending order of quantity down to one per cent, after which the order is the manufacturer's choice. So the first five or six names carry nearly all the meaning, and the long tail at the bottom carries almost none, whatever the front of the box has drawn your eye to.

Find the surfactant. Sodium lauryl sulphate and sodium laureth sulphate are the two most people have heard of, along with sodium C14-16 olefin sulphonate. On the pack they will be spelled the American way, sulfate, because ingredient names are standardised internationally regardless of where the product is sold. What matters is less whether they appear than where: second on the list is a different product from eighth.

Names like sodium palmate, sodium cocoate and sodium tallowate mean you are holding soap in the strict chemical sense, and soap is alkaline by definition. That is not a scandal. It is fine on many people's hands and bodies, and the face is a more demanding case. The gentler synthetic surfactants tend to have longer and less familiar names, among them cocamidopropyl betaine, sodium cocoyl isethionate and decyl glucoside. Their presence is a reasonable signal, not a promise; a formulation is a whole, and a mild surfactant can be undone by everything around it. Glycerin high on the list is generally a good sign.

Two things to read nothing into. Foam is one. Lather can be tuned almost independently of how stripping a blend is, so a cleanser that barely bubbles may be considerably harsher than one that fills your hands. The phrase pH balanced is the other, since it has no fixed legal meaning and no number attached. And be wary of choosing by the category printed on the front, because a fair amount of what people have filed under their own skin type turns out to be a cleanser they have been using without questioning it since they were nineteen.

sections.heading: Where this stops being about cleansers
paragraphs: If the tightness does not fade within an hour or two, or if skin is flaking, cracking, persistently sore or visibly inflamed, this article has run out of usefulness. That pattern is worth a doctor looking at it rather than a label. Several conditions present that way, none of them are a cleanser's business to sort out, and swapping products is at best a delay.

For everyone else the conclusion is smaller and duller than the internet would like it to be. A cleanser cannot transform anything. The most a well-made one can do is remove what was on your face and leave the skin looking and feeling roughly as it did before you started, which is an unglamorous bar and one that a surprising number of them fail to clear. We would rather say that than describe a rinse-off product as though it were a treatment.
So the test is the point, not the shopping. Ten minutes, five nights, nothing bought. Whatever your face tells you at the end of it is more useful than anything printed on a carton, including ours.

sources: It is long and uncontroversially established that the surface of healthy skin sits on the acid side of neutral, in the region of pH 4.5 to 5.5, and that true soaps are strongly alkaline by comparison.

The general finding that surfactants remove sebum along with some of the lipids and water-binding compounds of the outermost skin layer, and that water loss from the surface rises measurably after washing with harsher cleansers, is standard textbook skin chemistry rather than a novel result.
It is widely understood in skin biophysics that the outermost layer becomes stiffer and contracts slightly as it dries, which is the accepted mechanical explanation for the sensation of tightness.
Glycerin's behaviour as a humectant, drawing and holding water at the skin surface, has an unusually long and undisputed record and is not in serious scientific contention.

title: Starting Retinol Without the Peeling Weeks

article.lede: Retinoids are one of the few things in skincare where the evidence is genuinely strong, and one of the few where the first month is unpleasant enough that most people give up before anything interesting happens. The peeling everyone warns you about is not the ingredient working. It is the ingredient going faster than your skin can keep up with. Almost all of it is avoidable, and avoiding it costs nothing except patience.
article.meta_description: Retinoids work, but the first month puts most people off. How to introduce one so the adjustment stays quiet, and how to tell irritation from a warning.

sections.heading: What a retinoid actually is
paragraphs: Retinoid is a family name rather than a single ingredient. All of them are derivatives of vitamin A, and all of them have to end up as retinoic acid before the skin can do anything with them. Retinoic acid itself is a prescription medicine in most of Europe. Everything sold over the counter is a precursor that your skin converts, and the number of conversion steps is roughly the whole story: retinaldehyde is one step away, retinol is two, the esters like retinyl palmitate are further still. Fewer steps generally means faster results and a rougher introduction. More steps means gentler, slower, and at the far end gentle enough that not much happens at all.

What retinoids are understood to do is change the pace at which the surface layer renews itself and, over a longer span, influence the deeper layer where the structural fibres sit. That second part is the one worth waiting for. It is also the part that connects to the slow, unglamorous business of what happens to collagen from the mid-twenties onward. In terms of what you can see: texture looks finer, tone looks more even, and fine lines look softer under light that used to make them obvious.

Two honest limits. Nothing happens quickly — twelve weeks is the earliest point at which it is reasonable to judge a retinoid, and the changes people care about most take longer than that. And whatever a retinoid does overnight can be undone by a fortnight of unprotected sun, which makes daily sunscreen less a companion habit than a precondition. Retinoids are also prescribed as medicines for particular complaints, which is a conversation with a doctor rather than one an article can help with.

sections.heading: Why the first weeks go badly
paragraphs: The uncomfortable period has a name in dermatology, retinisation, and a simple explanation. The surface layer is being asked to turn over faster than the barrier underneath can be rebuilt. For a few weeks the skin runs a deficit. Water leaves faster than it should. Things that never used to sting, sting. The flaking usually shows up between day five and day fourteen, and it tends to start around the nose and the corners of the mouth, where the skin is thinner and folds constantly.

This is one of the few places in skincare where the phrase everyone uses loosely is literally accurate. Skin does adapt to a retinoid: the barrier catches up, the irritation subsides, and a frequency that was intolerable in week one becomes unremarkable by week six. It is worth being precise about that, because the idea that skin gets used to products is usually wrong in the way people mean it. Tolerance to irritation is real. The sense that a product has stopped working is almost always something else.

The belief that needs killing is that the peeling is the point. It is not the mechanism, it is the overshoot — visible evidence that the barrier lost the race. Plenty of people have used a retinoid steadily for years and never peeled once. They are not getting less out of it. They started slowly enough that the deficit never opened.

sections.heading: Frequency first, strength later
paragraphs: Most people get the order of the variables wrong. They buy the lowest strength on the shelf and then use it every single night, which is the one approach guaranteed to produce a bad month. Strength and frequency are both dials, and frequency is by far the more forgiving one to start with.

So: the lowest strength you can find, twice a week. If your skin reddens easily, once. Then hold. Four weeks of nothing happening — no flaking, no tightness the following morning, no stinging when you apply anything else — and you may move to every third night. Another four unremarkable weeks and you may move to alternate nights. If a step produces symptoms, drop back to the previous one and stay there longer. The whole ladder takes a season. That is the point rather than a flaw in it.

Nightly use is not the destination and it is not a mark of success. Two or three nights a week, indefinitely, is a legitimate place to stop climbing. Retinoids belong in the evening, both because light degrades many of them and because the evening is where repair-oriented work sits anyway. There is no version of this that goes in your morning routine.

sections.heading: Dry skin, a small amount, and a buffer
paragraphs: Apply it to dry skin. Not damp. The advice to apply things to damp skin is sound for humectants and unhelpful here, because damp skin takes up more of the product and takes it up faster, which is the opposite of what you want in the first two months. Cleanse, then wait ten to twenty minutes, until the face genuinely feels dry to the touch.

Use less than you think. A pea-sized amount covers an entire face, and that is not a figure of speech. Most people use three or four times as much, and more product accelerates nothing except the flaking.

Buffering is the other lever. Apply moisturiser first and the retinoid on top, or apply the retinoid and follow it immediately with moisturiser, or mix the two in your palm. All three slow delivery down. Purists will tell you buffering costs you something, and they are probably slightly right, and it does not matter at all if the alternative is abandoning the whole thing in week three. This is the one active worth breaking the usual sequence for; the ordinary logic of what goes on before what still governs everything else in the routine.

Two places deserve protection: the strip directly under the lower lashes, and the creases running from nose to mouth. Both collect product and both flake first. A thin layer of plain balm there beforehand works as a physical barrier. Keep the retinoid off the eyelids entirely.

sections.heading: What not to put on the same night
paragraphs: On a retinoid night the rest of the routine should be dull. No exfoliating acids, glycolic or lactic or salicylic. No scrub, no cloth, no brush, no clay mask, no peel of any kind however gentle the packaging sounds. If you use acids and want to keep them, they go on the nights the retinoid does not.

Vitamin C is best kept to the morning — not because of a chemistry problem, but because putting two irritants on one face on one evening is how people end up in trouble. The same reasoning covers benzoyl peroxide, strongly fragranced essences and toners, and anything sold as resurfacing. One active per evening will serve you well for the whole first year.

What is welcome on those nights: a plain moisturiser, niacinamide, ceramides, panthenol, squalane, an occlusive balm if the air is dry. Boring is precisely the goal. For the fortnight either side of starting or stepping up, be sensible about waxing, hair removal creams, and long unprotected days outdoors.

sections.heading: An adjustment, or a reason to stop
paragraphs: An adjustment looks like this: mild flaking a week or so in, a slight tightness in the morning that moisturiser resolves, a faint pink that has faded by midday, makeup catching on dry patches. Annoying rather than alarming, worst around week two, and at a fixed frequency it settles instead of escalating. If each week is a little easier than the last, you are passing through.

A reason to stop looks different, and the difference is obvious once you know to look for it. Plain water stings. The moisturiser you have used for years burns going on. The skin feels hot and tight and looks slightly glazed rather than dry and flaky. There is swelling, particularly around the eyes. There is itch instead of tightness, or weeping, crusting, or anything spreading beyond where you applied it. Burning that arrives before any flaking is a warning, not a phase. If you have reached the point where everything you own has started to sting, the retinoid is not the only thing to reconsider, but it is the first thing to remove.

The response is to stop completely rather than cut back. A gentle cleanser, one plain moisturiser, sunscreen in the morning, nothing else, for two weeks or until nothing stings, whichever is longer. Then begin again at half the frequency you were on when it went wrong. Restarting is not failure; it is the normal shape of this. A reaction that is painful, persistent or spreading is a matter for a doctor rather than a change of routine.

sections.heading: Why none of our six contains one
paragraphs: It is a fair question to put to us, given that this journal has repeatedly named retinoids as one of the few categories where the evidence earns the confidence around it. Six formulations, and no retinoid in any of them.

The reason is tolerance and layering, not scepticism. A retinoid reshapes the routine it enters. It dictates which nights are free, what can be applied alongside it, how much of anything else the skin will accept — and it asks for a difficult month before it gives anything back. We built our six to be used together, consistently, without a period of adjustment standing between someone and their own bathroom shelf. Those two goals pull in opposite directions and we chose the second deliberately.

That is a decision about fit, not a verdict on the ingredient. If you are already using a retinoid and it suits you, keep going. Nothing we make is intended to talk you out of it or to stand in for it. We would rather say plainly what we left out, and why, than imply the gap is a feature.

sources: Vitamin A derivatives are among the most extensively studied ingredients in dermatology. The general understanding is that they alter the rate at which the skin's surface layer renews itself, with visible change measured in months rather than weeks.

The irritation of the first weeks, commonly called retinisation, is well described in dermatological practice as a temporary consequence of surface turnover outpacing barrier repair, and as something that subsides at a fixed frequency.

It is broadly accepted that a compromised skin barrier loses water more quickly and reacts more readily to whatever is applied over it, which is why plain, unfragranced products are the standard advice during any adjustment period.
Cumulative ultraviolet exposure is generally accepted as the largest external contributor to how skin ages in appearance, which is why daily sun protection is standard advice alongside any retinoid.

title: Pores Don't Open and Close: What Actually Changes How They Look

article.meta_description: Pores have no muscle and cannot open or close. What actually changes how visible they look, which three habits help, and which two are only ritual.
article.lede: You cannot open a pore. You cannot close one either. There is nothing in there to open or close: no ring of muscle, no shutter, no valve. The whole vocabulary the industry uses around pores describes a mechanism that does not exist. What does exist is more interesting and more useful, because part of it you can influence and part of it was settled long before you bought your first cleanser.

sections.heading: What is actually down there
paragraphs: A facial pore is the opening of a hair follicle. Attached to the side of that follicle is a sebaceous gland, which makes oil and empties it into the shaft, and the oil travels up and out onto the surface. That is the entire apparatus. On the face the hair itself is usually so fine you never notice it, so what you see is the opening and whatever happens to be sitting in it.

There is no muscle around that opening. No sphincter, no valve, no ring of fibre that can tighten. The one muscle attached to a follicle is the arrector pili, which stands the hair up when you are cold or startled, and that is goosebumps. It does nothing to the width of the opening. Nothing in the structure is built to contract on cue, because nothing about the job requires it to.

Which leads somewhere unwelcome. The diameter of a follicle is set largely by inheritance and by how much oil moves through it, and no cream applied to the surface changes that number. What can change, genuinely and sometimes quite a lot, is how much of the opening you can see. Almost the entire perceived problem lives there.

sections.heading: Where opening and closing came from
paragraphs: The open-and-close vocabulary came out of the treatment room, and it came from something real. Steam a face for ten minutes and it behaves differently afterwards. Extractions get easier. It feels as though something has given way. What has actually softened is the contents: warm sebum is less viscous, and warm damp keratin swells and loosens its grip. The plug becomes moveable. The aperture is exactly where it was.

The cold rinse at the end is the other half of the ritual, and it also does something real, just not the advertised thing. Cold constricts the small vessels near the surface and briefly moves fluid out of the tissue, so the face looks less flushed and feels tighter for a while. It is the same effect as a chilled tool drawn across a puffy face in the morning, which is pleasant, visible, worth having, and entirely a matter of blood flow rather than follicles.

So temperature changes what you feel, and for an hour or two how the surface sits. It does not move the follicle wall in either direction. If the ritual leaves your skin looking better, believe your eyes. Just do not believe the explanation.

sections.heading: How full the pore is
paragraphs: The single biggest variable in how visible a pore looks on a given day is how full it is. An empty follicle in relaxed skin is close to invisible. One packed with sebum and shed cells sits proud, catches shadow at the rim, and reads as a dot from a metre away.

When the top of that plug meets air it oxidises and darkens. That is what people are describing when they say blackhead: not dirt, not something that arrived from outside, but the skin's own material sitting at the surface long enough to change colour. Worth saying plainly, because the dirt story sends people off to scrub, and scrubbing roughens the surrounding surface without emptying anything.

How quickly a follicle refills depends mostly on how much oil the skin makes, which is a matter of hormones, age and inheritance rather than discipline. This is one of the few places where knowing what your skin actually does is practically useful: high sebum output means pores fill within a day of cleansing, low output means they can be left alone for much longer, and neither is a verdict on your routine.

sections.heading: Light, tension and years
paragraphs: A pore is a small pit, and a pit is visible because of shadow. Change the light and you change the problem. Low, raking light from above or the side throws a shadow into every opening, which is why pores look their worst in a lift, a changing room, or a bathroom with a downlight directly over the mirror. Flat, diffuse light from in front fills those shadows and they largely vanish. The skin did not change in the thirty seconds between the two rooms.

The second variable is how taut the skin immediately around the opening is. Well-watered skin sits plump against itself and holds the rim looking neat; skin that has lost water at the surface slackens a little and lets the edges splay. This is real, and it is also temporary, which is more or less the definition of dehydration as opposed to dryness. A face that has been properly moisturised does show smaller-looking pores by the afternoon, and shows them again the next morning if the water has gone.

The third is slower and matters more. The opening keeps its shape because of the collagen and elastin packed around it. Decades of ultraviolet exposure degrade both, and the tissue that held the rim tidy loosens. This is why pores on sun-exposed cheeks often stretch from round into an elongated oval, tilted downwards. It is a marker of accumulated light, not of poor cleansing. It is also the only change on this list that does not reverse.

sections.heading: Three things that genuinely help
paragraphs: Cleanse twice a day, and do it without stripping. The point is to stop the follicle filling and oxidising, which means removing oil and the day's residue reliably rather than aggressively. A cleanser that leaves the face feeling tight has taken more than it needed to, and stripped skin looks duller and slightly rough, which does the shadow problem no favours at all.

Exfoliate on a schedule you can defend. Salicylic acid is oil-soluble, so it can get into the follicle rather than only working across the top of it, and at sensible intervals it keeps the contents from consolidating. The temptation is always to do more, and that is where most people come unstuck; the frequency question deserves proper thought, and measured exfoliation beats daily exfoliation more often than the shelf would have you believe. Retinoids are the other well-studied route to smoother-looking surface texture over months, though again the effect is on how the surface reads, not on the width of anything.

Protect from the sun, every day, for years. This is the least satisfying advice on the page, because none of it pays off this month. But the loosening of the structure around the follicle is what makes pores look permanently larger rather than temporarily so, and ultraviolet exposure is the main driver of it. Making sun protection an unremarkable daily habit will not shrink a pore. It protects the tissue that keeps the rim tidy, and over a decade that is the more valuable thing by a distance.

sections.heading: Two things that are theatre
paragraphs: The first is the steam-then-cold-water sequence sold as opening and closing. The steaming half is defensible as preparation, since softened contents genuinely help if someone trained is about to perform extractions. The cold half does nothing except feel decisive. And a long session of hot steam leaves plenty of people flushed and slightly irritated-looking for the rest of the evening, which is the opposite of what was wanted.

The second is pore strips and peel-off masks. They work in the narrow sense that they remove the top few millimetres of a plug and let you look at it afterwards, which is exactly why they are so satisfying. What they do not do is change the follicle. The gland keeps producing, the opening refills within days, and repeated aggressive removal can leave the skin around it looking red and roughened, which makes each opening catch more shadow rather than less.

The same logic covers astringent toners marketed as pore-minimising. Alcohol dehydrates the surface, dehydrated skin tightens briefly, and the effect lasts about as long as the sting. Nothing has happened to the follicle. Something has happened to your skin's water, and not in the direction you wanted.

sections.heading: The honest limit of this
paragraphs: Here is the summary nobody standing behind a counter is incentivised to give you. Pore size is mostly inherited. Oil output, which fills them, is mostly hormonal. Sun exposure, which loosens the structure around them, is cumulative and partly already spent. Between those three, most of what determines how your pores look was decided before you chose a cleanser.

What is left is not nothing. Keeping them empty, keeping the surrounding skin watered, and protecting the structure from further light all genuinely change how much shadow a face collects, and shadow is what you are actually looking at in the mirror. That is a narrower claim than the category usually makes. It is also the one that survives contact with the evidence.

One boundary worth naming. Congestion that is persistent, painful or inflamed rather than simply visible is a medical question and belongs with a doctor, not a skincare counter. Nothing described here is a treatment for anything.

We are writing this before we have anything to sell: six formulations in development, none of them on a shelf, no ingredient list published and no study completed. That makes the honest version easier to write. We would rather set the position now than promise something the skin was never going to do.

sources: What is generally understood about the anatomy of a facial pore: it is the surface opening of a hair follicle with a sebaceous gland attached, and the structure contains no muscular ring able to narrow or widen it. The only muscle attached to a follicle is the one that raises the hair.

It is broadly accepted in dermatology that how large a pore appears tracks with sebum output, and that sebum output is governed largely by hormones, age and inherited factors rather than by cleansing habits.

The degradation of dermal collagen and elastin by cumulative ultraviolet exposure is among the most consistently reproduced findings in skin science, and is the usual explanation given for the elongated, oval pore shape seen on long sun-exposed areas such as the cheeks.
The effects of temperature on skin are generally described in terms of blood flow and the viscosity of sebum, not in terms of any change to the diameter of a follicle.

title: Hard Water and Your Skin: What the Tap Is Actually Doing

article.meta_description: Hard water is dissolved calcium and magnesium. Its effect on skin is real but narrower than filter marketing suggests, and mostly about rinsing.
article.lede: If you have moved house and found that your skin changed with the postcode, you were not imagining it. Water hardness varies enormously over short distances, and it does change how washing feels. But the effect is narrower than the filter market would like, and it is mostly not about minerals touching your face. It is about what those minerals do to your cleanser on the way down the drain.

sections.heading: Hardness, defined
paragraphs: Hard water is water carrying dissolved calcium and magnesium, picked up from the rock it has travelled through. Chalk and limestone dissolve readily. Granite barely dissolves at all. That is the whole mechanism, and it explains why a kettle in Kent furs up in a month while the same kettle in the Scottish Highlands can go years without a mark.

Hardness is measured as milligrams of calcium carbonate per litre, though several competing scales exist and your water supplier will publish a figure for your postcode. The line at which water starts being called hard sits somewhere between 120 and 180 milligrams per litre depending on whose scale you are reading. Below about 60, it is soft.
None of this is mysterious and none of it is new. What is new is the volume of marketing built on top of it.

sections.heading: The residue, not the minerals
paragraphs: Calcium and magnesium ions react with the fatty acid salts in true soap to form compounds that will not dissolve. That is soap scum. The ring around the bath, the film on the shower screen, the dullness on a glass out of the dishwasher. The same reaction happens on your face. Part of the cleanser precipitates instead of rinsing, and it stays where it landed.

That residue is what most people are describing when they say hard water dries them out. It sits on the surface. It does not hold water the way a moisturiser does, and left there it can behave as a mild irritant. If you have wondered why your face feels tight in the minutes after washing, this is a large part of the answer, and it is the part nobody sells you a device for.

The minerals on their own are doing far less than they are given credit for. Calcium at domestic concentrations is not stripping your barrier. Where hard water does appear to make matters worse, it is in combination with a surfactant, which makes it a rinsing problem rather than a mineral-contact problem. The distinction matters, because the two point at completely different fixes.

sections.heading: The same cleanser in two cities
paragraphs: Take a bar of soap from a soft-water town to a hard-water one and it stops lathering properly. Same bar, same hands, different result. So you use more of it, and you rinse for longer, and you finish with more residue on your skin than you started out trying to remove. This is the practical form the problem takes, and it is why people conclude a product has been quietly reformulated when nothing has changed but the tap.

The intuitive geography, though, is wrong. London and Barcelona are both hard. London draws heavily on a chalk aquifer and sits at the very hard end of European supplies; Barcelona's water carries a different load, higher in chlorides and sulphates from the ground its rivers run through. Neither city is anywhere near soft. What differs between them is the character of the water rather than the presence of hardness, and then everything that happens to skin after the shower, which is a matter of humidity, sun and salt air rather than plumbing.

So when a cleanser that suited you in one place feels wrong in another, hardness is one variable among several and rarely the loudest. How hot you run the water, how long you stand under it, and what the air does to your skin for the following twelve hours are all competing for the same explanation.

sections.heading: Where the evidence stops
paragraphs: There is a substantial body of population research linking the hardness of domestic water to a higher prevalence of atopic skin conditions in young children. It has turned up in several countries with different climates and different health systems, which is the kind of consistency that deserves to be taken seriously rather than waved away.

What happened next is the part that rarely gets quoted. When water softeners were actually installed and tested against ordinary care, the improvement the association implied did not clearly appear. Reasonable people still disagree about why. The honest reading is that hardness may be one contributing exposure among many, and that softening the supply does not reliably undo it. Skin that is persistently cracked, itching or inflamed is a matter for a doctor, not for a shower fitting and not for a cream.

For an adult with no diagnosis and no unusual sensitivity, the effect of hard water is real, modest, and cosmetic in the literal sense of the word. It changes how skin looks and feels in the half hour after washing. That is a smaller claim than the one usually made, and it happens to be the true one.

sections.heading: What a shower filter can and cannot remove
paragraphs: Most shower filters contain a copper-zinc alloy medium, activated carbon, ascorbic acid, or some combination of the three. These are genuinely effective against chlorine, and chlorine is mildly drying, so people who notice a difference after fitting one are usually not imagining that either. If your supply is heavily chlorinated and you can smell it at the tap, a filter is a defensible small purchase.

What almost none of them do is soften water. Removing calcium and magnesium requires ion exchange: a resin bed that swaps the hardness ions for sodium and has to be regenerated periodically with salt. That is a plumbed appliance with a brine tank in a cupboard, not a cartridge screwed onto a shower arm. The small in-line cartridges sold as softeners do contain resin, but the volume of resin is tiny against the volume of a shower, and it exhausts far faster than the packaging implies.

So the honest summary is unglamorous. A shower filter may reduce chlorine, which some skins appreciate. It will not meaningfully change your water's hardness. A whole-house softener will, at the cost of installation, maintenance, salt and a small rise in the sodium content of the supply, and the strongest arguments for one concern your boiler and your kettle rather than your face.

sections.heading: What actually helps
paragraphs: Change the cleanser before you change the plumbing. True soap is the ingredient that reacts with hardness, so the swap that matters is away from soap and towards a synthetic detergent cleanser: the non-soap bars, and most gels, milks and creams. They do not form the same insoluble film, and they rinse out of hard water far more completely. It is a smaller intervention than a filter, it costs less, and it addresses the actual chemistry rather than the story around it.

Then the boring things, which are boring because they work. Cooler water. Less time under it. Fewer washes than instinct suggests, since the case for cleansing twice a day is thinner than most routines assume. And moisturise while the skin is still damp, before the residue and the evaporation have finished their work.

If you want a cheap diagnostic, wash your face once at the sink with bottled or filtered water and pay attention to the ten minutes that follow. It is not a controlled experiment and you should not treat it as one. But it will tell you, for the price of a bottle of water, whether the tap is a variable worth spending real money on.

sections.heading: A different question about water
paragraphs: We think about water more than most houses do, so it is worth being precise about which question we are answering. Our interest is in what a water carries: why we build the formulations on a specific mineral water rather than a purified blank, and how altitude and rock determine what a spring picks up on the way down. That is a question about composition inside a bottle, at a known quantity, in a known formula.

A tap is a different problem entirely. There the water is uncontrolled, it varies by postcode and by season, and most of its effect on your skin is mediated by whatever you dissolved into it thirty seconds earlier. Choosing a mineral water base is not a defence against your shower, and we would be overreaching to imply that it were. Different question, different answer.

The honest limit of this subject is that hard water is a small, real, largely rinse-related variable in how skin looks and feels. Get the cleanser right and it mostly stops mattering. If it does not stop mattering, the answer is probably not in the water.

sources: It is long-established basic chemistry that the calcium and magnesium ions responsible for water hardness react with fatty acid soaps to form insoluble salts, the film commonly known as soap scum, while synthetic detergents largely do not.
It is generally understood in hydrogeology that hardness reflects the rock a supply has passed through: chalk and limestone catchments yield hard water, granite catchments yield soft water.

A consistent body of population research has reported an association between domestic water hardness and a higher prevalence of atopic skin conditions in young children, while trials that actually installed softeners did not show a matching benefit. The question is generally regarded as unsettled.

It is well established that surfactant contact temporarily raises the pH of the skin surface and increases water loss through it, and that the effect is greater when washing is prolonged or the water is hot.

title: When Everything Suddenly Stings

article.lede: It arrives without warning, though it was never sudden. One morning the serum you have used for a year goes on and your cheeks light up. Not a rash, not a burn. Just a bright, unfriendly sting that fades in a minute and leaves you standing at the sink wondering what you did. Then the moisturiser does it too. Then plain water. Nothing in your routine changed, which is precisely the problem.
article.meta_description: Why products that were fine last month suddenly sting, what a compromised skin barrier means in plain terms, and the slow, dull way back to comfort.

sections.heading: What the barrier actually is
paragraphs: The outermost layer of your skin is roughly as thick as clingfilm. It is made of flattened cells that are no longer alive, stacked in overlapping sheets and held together by a mixture of fats — ceramides, cholesterol, fatty acids. Bricks and mortar is the usual comparison and it is a decent one. The job of this layer is unglamorous: keep water in, keep most of the outside world out.

When people say the barrier is compromised, what they mean is that the mortar has gone thin and patchy in places. Water leaves faster than it should. Things that were meant to stay on the surface get slightly further in than they were designed to, and the nerve endings below get more of the message than they would otherwise. That is the sting. It is not the product doing something new. It is the same product arriving somewhere it did not used to reach.

The honest limit of this is that you cannot see any of it. The barrier is a model — a useful, well-supported model, but not a thing you can inspect in the bathroom mirror. What you actually have is a pattern: a sensation that was not there before, and a look that has shifted. Skin that has been through this tends to look flushed rather than evenly pink, and shiny in a thin, papery way rather than dewy. One stinging morning is not evidence of anything. Three weeks of them is.

sections.heading: The causes are cumulative and dull
paragraphs: Almost everyone looks for a culprit. A new bottle, a bad batch, something that arrived in the post last Tuesday. Usually there isn't one. What there is, instead, is arithmetic. An acid twice a week. A retinoid three nights. Vitamin C every morning. A clay mask on Sundays because Sunday feels like the day for it. Each of those is defensible on its own, and taken together they leave the skin no days off at all. The damage is not dramatic; it is a slow overdraft.

Then there is the cleanser, which is almost never suspected, because it is on your face for forty seconds and then it is gone. But it is the only product in the routine whose entire purpose is to remove things, and you use it twice a day, every day, for years. If yours leaves you with that tight, squeaky feeling once the water is off, it has been taking slightly more than it should the whole time. Nobody notices, because it never stings. It just quietly raises the floor of everything else.

Non-product life contributes too, and gets less credit than it deserves. A winter of dry indoor heating. Showers hot enough to redden the face. A fortnight of bad sleep, a long flight, a new prescription from your GP. Skin is a record of the last month rather than the last night, which is why the timing never seems to line up with anything you can name.

sections.heading: How this differs from ordinary dryness
paragraphs: Dry skin wants moisturiser and is grateful when it gets it. That is the whole test, really. If a plain cream goes on and things immediately feel better, you are dry. If a plain cream goes on and your face objects for thirty seconds first, something else is happening. The distinguishing feature here is not dryness. It is reactivity — the skin has stopped being able to tell the difference between an ingredient and an insult.

The look changes in ways that are easier to notice on photographs than in the mirror. Foundation that used to sit flat starts clinging to small rough patches by midday. Fine lines around the eyes and across the forehead look more obvious than they did in the spring, because skin holding less water creases more readily and holds the crease longer. Colour concentrates around the nose and the inner cheeks. None of this is permanent, and none of it means the underlying structure has changed. It means the surface is not holding water well.

One more clue: it is usually worst exactly where you have been most diligent. The cheeks, which get the serum. The area around the nose, which gets the extra pass with the cleanser. Not the neck, which gets whatever is left on your hands.

sections.heading: The smallest possible routine, for two weeks
