If you want the underlying mechanism in more detail, we have written about the slow arithmetic of collagen loss at greater length, and it sits inside the broader picture of how skin ages rather than replacing it.

What you see is a consequence of less structural support underneath. Skin looks thinner and reads as less springy. Lines that used to settle overnight now hold their shape. The jaw softens and the cheek loses a little of its lift. Texture on the neck can take on the fine crumpled look people call crepey. None of this is sudden, though it is often noticed suddenly, usually in unflattering light in a hotel bathroom.

sections.heading: Oil, water, and the tight feeling by mid-afternoon
paragraphs: Sebum production tends to fall in this period, and for many women it falls quite sharply. There is a particular disorientation in it for anyone who spent two decades managing shine. The skin goes matte, which is briefly satisfying, and then it goes tight. The oil that was such a nuisance was doing real work, sitting on the surface and slowing the rate at which water left the skin all day.

Two quite different things get called dry skin, and confusing them wastes a lot of money. One is a shortage of oil. The other is a shortage of water in the outer layers, which can happen on any skin at any age, including oily skin. The distinction between dryness and dehydration matters more now than it did before, because perimenopause can hand you both at once, which is why a single rich cream sometimes only half solves it.

The most useful early change is usually subtraction rather than addition. A foaming cleanser that was fine at thirty-five can strip a skin producing less oil at forty-eight. Very hot water does the same. Before adding a fifth step, take away the thing that leaves your face feeling squeaky, because squeaky is the sound of a barrier that has just been stripped of the lipids holding its water in.

sections.heading: Skin that used to tolerate everything
paragraphs: The other common complaint is reactivity. Products that lived on the shelf for years begin to sting. Skin flushes more easily, stays flushed longer, and takes its time settling after a wind, a hot room or a glass of wine. A barrier that recovers more slowly is less forgiving, and the acid you used twice a week without a thought is now doing more than you intended.

There is a limit to what this article can responsibly say here. Persistent redness, a rash, burning that does not settle, a patch that behaves differently from the skin around it, any change in a mole: these are not skincare questions. Several genuine medical conditions present as what people call sensitive skin, they are diagnosed by a doctor, and they are treated by a doctor. Reaching for a gentler serum instead of an appointment is the wrong instrument for the job.

For ordinary reactivity, the approach is dull and it works. Strip the routine back to a cleanser, a moisturiser and a sunscreen for a fortnight. Reintroduce one active at a time, with a week between, patch tested on the jawline first. You are gathering information about a skin that has genuinely changed, which means old knowledge about what suits you may simply be out of date.

sections.heading: What skincare can honestly do
paragraphs: Topical skincare works on the outer layers of the skin and on appearance. That is a real limit, and it is also less trivial than it sounds. A great deal of what reads on a face as tired is happening in the top fraction of a millimetre: water content in the surface layer, the evenness of the texture, how light scatters off it rather than reflecting cleanly. Change those and the face looks different, because looking different is what those things are for.

The categories with the longest-standing evidence behind them are unglamorous. Daily sun protection is the largest lever anyone has over how skin looks in ten years. A moisturiser that supports the barrier, with humectants to hold water and lipids to slow its escape, addresses the complaint most women in this decade actually have. Retinoids remain among the best-evidenced ingredients for the appearance of lines and texture over months, with a real cost in irritation, and irritation is what a reactive skin has least appetite for. Vitamin C and niacinamide sit in the sensible middle: worth using, oversold everywhere.

Here is the honest limit of all of it. Nothing you apply to the surface of your face addresses the hormonal change underneath. A cream does not restore oestrogen signalling in the dermis, and any brand implying that its formula balances your hormones has left the territory of cosmetics entirely. What good skincare does is change how skin looks and feels while the transition happens on its own schedule. That is worth doing. It is not the same thing as treating it.

sections.heading: Where the line sits
paragraphs: There are medical approaches to this transition, they are well established, and they are not our subject. They belong in a consulting room with someone who knows your history and can weigh benefit against risk for you specifically. A skincare house has no business steering that decision in either direction, and any that does should be read with suspicion.

It is also worth acknowledging how thin the skin-specific research is compared with the confidence people express about it. Much of what exists is small, short, and run on volunteers who do not much resemble the general population. The broad direction of travel is reasonably certain. The details, the timings, the individual variation, are far less settled than the marketing suggests.

The parts of this that most affect how skin looks may not be cosmetic at all. Sleep that fragments, months of it, shows on a face more plainly than any serum corrects. So do the temperature swings that interrupt it. Those are worth raising with a doctor for their own sake, and your skin is one more reason to.

sections.heading: A routine that changes when you do
paragraphs: Start by accepting that the category you have filed yourself under for twenty years may no longer apply. Plenty of women in this decade are still using products built for a skin type they no longer have, which is worth reassessing honestly rather than assuming. Combination skin becomes dry skin. Oily skin becomes normal skin that is dehydrated by the routine designed to keep it in check.

Extend whatever you do below the jaw. The neck, chest and hands show this stretch of years earlier and more plainly than the face does, partly because there is less oil and thinner skin to begin with, and partly because thirty years of diligent facial sunscreen have often stopped at the chin. It costs nothing to carry the same products further down.

Then be patient in a way the industry does not encourage. Skin turnover takes weeks and dermal change takes considerably longer, so judge a routine over seasons rather than a fortnight, and photograph yourself in the same light if you want to see anything real. The mirror is a poor instrument for measuring slow change, and a worse one at seven in the morning.

We are still in the laboratory in Barcelona, and when our formulations are ready we will describe them the way we have described everything here: in terms of how skin looks and how it feels. That is the claim we can stand behind. The part happening underneath is yours and your doctor's, and no cream has a legitimate opinion about it.

sources: It is generally understood in dermatological research that skin collagen content and dermal thickness decline gradually across adult life, and that the years surrounding menopause represent a faster phase of that decline. The size of the effect varies considerably between individuals and between studies, and the commonly quoted figures carry more precision than the underlying evidence supports.

Sebum production is broadly understood to decrease with age in women, with a more marked reduction after menopause. This is a long-standing observation across measurement studies rather than the finding of any single trial.

The role of cumulative ultraviolet exposure as the largest external contributor to the visible signs of skin ageing is among the most consistently supported findings in the field, and is not specific to any stage of life.

Barrier function, assessed as the rate at which water is lost through the skin, is generally understood to become less efficient with age, though individual variation, climate and cleansing habits influence it substantially.

title: Shaving and the Skin Barrier: A Formulator's View

article.lede: Most people who shave do it three or four times a week and never once file it under exfoliation. It belongs there. A razor is a blade drawn across skin under pressure, and hair is not the only thing it takes off. If you also use an acid, or a retinoid, or a weekly peel, this matters. Not because shaving is bad for your skin, but because you are almost certainly counting wrong.
article.meta_description: Shaving is exfoliation, whether or not you count it that way. What a blade removes, how it interacts with acids, and what actually reduces irritation.

sections.heading: What a blade actually takes off
paragraphs: A razor is a hard edge held at an angle and drawn across a surface that is not flat. Hair grows out of follicles sitting below that surface, so to cut a hair close to the skin the edge has to travel along the skin itself. It does not hover. What ends up rinsed down the sink is hair and, with it, some of the outermost layer of skin: the stratum corneum, a few dozen cells thick, made of flattened dead cells that were on their way off anyway.

How much? This is where honesty is more useful than confidence. It depends on the blade, the pressure, the number of passes, how hydrated the skin was and whose skin it is. Nobody can hand you a figure that would mean anything for your own face on a Tuesday morning. What can be said is that the effect is real, repeated, and comparable in kind to a gentle physical exfoliant, which is a strange thing to do four times a week without noticing.

The removal is also not selective. A blade cannot tell a cell that has finished its work from one still holding water in. An enzyme or an acid can, more or less. A razor cannot. That does not make shaving harmful, because the stratum corneum is built to shed and rebuild and it does exactly that. It means the skin is doing repair work on a schedule you set, and it would help to know you set it.

sections.heading: The exfoliation you are not counting
paragraphs: Add it up. Four shaves a week. A weekly peel or acid treatment. A retinoid most evenings. A body scrub on Sunday. Each of those is a nudge to the surface, and the skin does not file them separately. It registers only that the outer layer keeps being interrupted before it has finished settling.

This journal has argued for a while that weekly exfoliation does more for skin than daily scrubbing, and the argument holds here with one adjustment. If you shave regularly, part of that weekly allowance is already spent. Not all of it: a shave takes off less than a proper exfoliating treatment, and it only touches the area you shaved. But it is not zero, and treating it as zero is how people end up wondering why an acid that was fine last month now stings.

The practical version is unglamorous. Do not exfoliate the same patch of skin on the same day you shave it. If you shave your face most mornings, put the peel on an evening after a day you skipped. If you shave your legs in the shower, that is not the shower for the body scrub.

sections.heading: Softening does more than the blade does
paragraphs: Hair is mostly keratin, and keratin takes up water. Hydrated hair is substantially softer and easier to cut than dry hair. This is one of the better established things in the whole subject and it is the largest lever most people are not pulling. A softer hair needs less force at the edge. Less force means fewer passes. Fewer passes means less of the skin surface comes away with the hair.

In practice that means a few minutes, not a few seconds. Shave at the end of a shower rather than the start. Or hold a warm, wet flannel against the area for a minute or two beforehand and let it actually work. Splashing water on your face and reaching straight for the razor is doing very little.

Shaving creams, gels and oils are useful, and their useful job is narrower than the packaging suggests. They provide slip, so the edge glides rather than drags, and they slow the water leaving the hair while you work. That is worth having. It is not worth agonising over. The gap between a good preparation and a mediocre one is much smaller than the gap between softened skin and unsoftened skin.

sections.heading: Where the razor sits in the order
paragraphs: Cleanse first. A blade dragged across a day of sebum, sunscreen and city air is a blade that skips and clogs, and you will compensate for that with pressure. But the choice of cleanser matters more than the order does. If your face is tight and squeaking before you have even picked up the razor, that is the wrong cleanser to be shaving behind. Tightness is the barrier reporting that it has been stripped, and stripped skin does not need a blade next.

Afterwards, the surface is briefly more permeable than usual. Water leaves it faster and whatever you apply gets in more readily, which sounds like an opportunity and is mostly a trap. This is the wrong moment for the strongest product you own. It is a good moment for something plain: a light, unfragranced hydrating layer, and then whatever order you normally apply things in, with the actives moved later or moved off the day altogether.

Across the day, the cleanest separation is the one this journal already recommends for other reasons, which is letting the morning and the evening do different jobs. Shave in the morning. Keep the acids and the retinoid for the night. Twelve hours is not a magic number, but it is enough for the surface to have stopped complaining.

sections.heading: What actually reduces irritation
paragraphs: In rough order of how much difference each one makes: a sharp blade, light pressure, fewer passes, short strokes, and rinsing the blade between them. None of that is interesting and all of it matters more than anything you can buy to put on afterwards.

A dull blade is the most common cause of a bad shave and the easiest thing to fix. It needs more force to cut the same hair, which means more pressure on the skin, which means more of the surface comes away and more of the hair gets tugged rather than cut. Replacing the blade more often than feels necessary is the cheapest improvement available anywhere in this article.

Blade count is oversold. More edges do mean each one can do less work, but they also mean more edges crossing the same patch of skin in a single stroke. That is a trade, not a free upgrade, and people whose skin is easily irritated often do better with fewer. Direction is a similar trade. With the grain is gentler, against the grain is closer, and very few people need the closest possible result every single day.

Two things help less than their marketing implies. Stretching the skin taut to get closer lifts the hair so it is cut below the surface line, which is precisely the geometry that causes some people trouble a few days later. And an aftershave that stings is not disinfecting anything. Alcohol on a surface you have just abraded is a sensation, not a treatment.

sections.heading: Legs, underarms and everything else
paragraphs: None of this is about faces particularly. The skin does not know which part of the body it is on, or whose. The same blade physics applies to a shin, an underarm, a chest, a scalp.

Legs take the largest number of passes over the largest area, usually at the end of a shower, which is accidentally the right time. The skin and the hair have had ten minutes of warm water by then. Most complaints about leg shaving come from doing it dry, or first thing, or with a blade that has been sitting in a wet shower rack for six weeks. The rack does more harm to the blade than the shaving does to you.

Underarms are the harder case. That skin is thinner, it sits in a fold, it is covered by clothing all day, it is in constant friction, and most people apply an antiperspirant to it within about ninety seconds of shaving. If that stings, it is not a sign of anything working. It is a product arriving on a surface that has just been exfoliated. Leaving a gap, or shaving at night and applying in the morning, removes most of the problem for most people.
The arithmetic from earlier applies to bodies too. A scrub, a self tan, a retinoid body lotion and a shave in the same evening is four interventions on one surface. Choose one.

sections.heading: Where this stops being a routine question
paragraphs: Some things a shaving technique will not fix. Persistent bumps along the jaw or the bikini line, hairs that curl back into the skin, inflammation that does not settle within a day. These have proper names, real causes, and answers that come from a doctor rather than from a bathroom cabinet. It is worth saying plainly, because there is a whole shelf of products sold on the implication that they are a skincare problem. They are not.

Short of that, the general rule holds. If your skin has reached the point where everything you apply stings, shaving belongs on the list of things to pause, alongside the acid and the retinoid. Pausing it is not a defeat. It is a week.

The narrow, true version of all this: shaving is not bad for your skin. It is an exfoliation you were not counting, performed with a tool that cannot be selective, on skin that is usually less prepared than it should be. Improve the preparation, count the exfoliation honestly, and replace the blade more often. That is most of it. The rest is a question of what you put on afterwards, and less of that matters than the industry would like you to think.

sources: What is generally understood about the outermost layer of skin: the stratum corneum is a few dozen layers of flattened dead cells that shed continually and are replaced from below, and mechanical contact with the surface, a razor included, takes some of them with it.

What is generally understood about hair mechanics: hair is largely keratin, keratin softens measurably as it takes up water, and softened hair requires less force to cut. This is the long-standing reason warm water and a few minutes of waiting are recommended before shaving.

What is generally understood about barrier disruption: it is conventionally observed as a temporary rise in water lost through the skin after the surface has been abraded, settling again as the barrier rebuilds over the following days.

What is generally understood about skin renewal: the full turnover cycle is usually described as roughly a month in young adults and longer with age, which is the general reason exfoliating treatments are better spaced out than stacked together.

title: Sweat, Friction and the Gym: What Exercise Does to Skin

article.lede: Type the question into a search bar and the answers come back with real confidence. Sweat flushes the pores. Sweat pushes toxins out. A hard session is a facial from the inside. None of it is true. What exercise does for skin is real, but it happens somewhere else entirely, and it does not happen on the timescale of a single workout — which is, admittedly, a less satisfying thing to be told.
article.meta_description: Sweat does not detoxify skin or clean pores. What exercise genuinely does, what actually causes post-workout breakouts, and what to do afterwards.

sections.heading: What sweat actually is
paragraphs: Sweat is mostly water. Sodium and chloride, a little potassium, some urea and lactate, traces of other things — but overwhelmingly water. Most of it comes from eccrine glands, which sit almost everywhere on the body and open directly onto the surface. The armpits and groin also carry apocrine glands, which produce something thicker and protein-rich that skin bacteria then act on, which is where body odour actually comes from. The purpose of the whole arrangement is temperature. Water evaporating off skin carries heat away with it. That is the design brief, and sweat is very good at it.

The detox claim survives because it sounds plausible and nobody checks it. The body does have an elimination system and it is the liver and the kidneys. Sweat carries small amounts of urea and trace metals, but the quantities are negligible beside what leaves in urine every day. Treating a spin class as a route of elimination gets the arithmetic wrong by a wide margin. You are not unloading anything your kidneys were not already handling before you got on the bike.

Notice, too, that the word toxins is never attached to an actual molecule. Ask which one and the conversation moves elsewhere. That is usually the sign of a claim assembled backwards from a feeling — you feel wrung out and virtuous after training, and the feeling wants an explanation.

sections.heading: Sweat does not clean your pores
paragraphs: Start with the anatomy, because the myth depends on getting it wrong. The pore you can see on your nose is the opening of a hair follicle with a sebaceous gland attached to it, and sebum comes up that channel. Eccrine sweat ducts are separate structures, much narrower, opening onto the surface on their own. Sweat is not travelling up through the follicle and pushing a plug of sebum ahead of it. There is no plunger.

What people notice is real, though. Ten minutes in, the face flushes, because blood flow to the skin rises to shed heat and the small vessels dilate. Skin looks fuller, more even in colour, slightly plumper — mild transient swelling softens the look of fine lines much as a hot shower does. It is a genuine effect. It lasts twenty minutes to an hour or two, and then it goes.

One honest footnote. Sweat is slightly acidic and contains antimicrobial peptides, which is well established and reasonably interesting. It is not a cleansing mechanism, and it does not make sweat a substitute for washing. The distance between sweat has some antimicrobial properties and sweat cleans your face is roughly the space this entire myth lives in.

sections.heading: What exercise genuinely does for skin
paragraphs: Circulation is the first real thing. Regular aerobic exercise improves how well the vascular system works, and skin is a densely vascularised organ. Better vascular function means more reliable delivery to the tissue and better clearance away from it. This is cumulative and slow. It is a property of training over months, not a property of the hour after training.

Sleep is the second, and it may be the largest. The link between regular physical activity and better sleep quality is one of the sturdier findings in the field, and it matters here because skin does most of its repair work overnight. Someone who has slept well for a year looks different from someone who has not.
Stress is the third. Over months, regular activity lowers the body's baseline stress response, and chronically raised cortisol is not kind to how skin looks.

None of this will show up by Tuesday. It belongs to the same unexciting category as the everyday habits that shape how skin ages: individually modest, collectively the thing that decides the outcome. The industry sells the flush and ignores the circulation, because the flush photographs well and circulation does not.

sections.heading: Friction, occlusion and sweat left sitting
paragraphs: If sweat is not the culprit, what is? Mostly friction. Consider what touches your face in an hour: a chin on a mat, a helmet strap, a damp headband, a bar resting on the shoulder, a phone against a wet cheek, and your own hands wiping the forehead over and over. Warm, damp skin is softer skin, and softer skin abrades more easily. It is the same category of small repeated mechanical insult as dragging a blade across the face every morning: individually trivial, cumulatively not.

Then occlusion. Tight synthetic fabrics hold heat and moisture against the skin for the length of the session and often long after it. Warm, damp and enclosed is the condition under which the skin's resident microbes are happiest, and it is no coincidence that the complaints cluster on the back, the chest and the line of a sports bra strap rather than on exposed forearms.

Then sweat left sitting. Sweat that evaporates is doing its job. Sweat that dries on the skin leaves its salt behind, and salt on a softened barrier is a low-grade irritant. Add the drive home in the same damp kit, some errands, a shower two hours later, and you have most of the mechanism people attribute to sweat itself. The problem is not the sweat. It is the sitting.

One caveat that matters. Persistent, inflamed or spreading skin problems are not a laundry issue, and some genuine conditions are aggravated by heat and friction in ways no washing routine will settle. Working out which is which is a conversation with a doctor, not with an article.

sections.heading: Heavy makeup and heavy sweat
paragraphs: The combination worth naming is heavy base makeup, heavy sweat and an hour of friction. Foundation is engineered to sit on the surface and stay there. Heat, moisture and a forearm across the forehead defeat that engineering, and what you get is product moved around and pressed into places it was not sitting before, on skin that is warm, softened and rubbing against equipment.

This is not a moral point. If wearing makeup is the difference between going and not going, wear the makeup; the training is worth more than the compromise. But lighter is genuinely better here, a tinted sunscreen is a sensible substitute for outdoor sessions, and taking it off soon after you finish matters more than what you take it off with.
For anyone training outdoors, the more consequential exposure is not the foundation anyway. It is the midday sun, four times a week, for years.

sections.heading: Before and after, in the order that matters
paragraphs: Before a session, the useful instruction is less. Clean skin, nothing heavy, no thick occlusive layer under a helmet. Skip acids and retinoids immediately beforehand — applying something designed to make skin more reactive and then heating it, sweating on it and rubbing it against a mat is a reliable way to end up sore. If you are training outdoors, sunscreen. That is the one item on the before list that genuinely earns its place.

Afterwards, wash reasonably promptly. Not frantically, not within ninety seconds. Within the hour is fine, and the difference between showering straight away and showering an hour later is much smaller than the difference between one hour and four. Lukewarm water, a gentle cleanser, hands rather than a flannel. This single habit is worth more than any product applied afterwards, and it costs nothing, which is an awkward thing for a skincare house to write down and still true.

The rest is logistics. Get out of damp kit rather than sitting in it. Use a clean towel, and a clean headband, more often than feels necessary. Wipe equipment down before your face goes near it. And do not scrub. The urge to scour after sweating is understandable and exactly wrong, because it takes an abrasive to a barrier that has just spent an hour being softened and rubbed.

If your skin has already reached the stage where everything you apply seems to sting, the post-workout answer is less rather than more: rinse, something bland, and nothing with an active in it for a while.

sections.heading: The honest limit of all this
paragraphs: The variation between people here is wider than the confidence around it. Some find that three months of regular training visibly changes how their skin looks, in the direction they wanted. Others find that training brings on congestion however quickly they wash. Both are ordinary, and neither tells you much about anyone else.

What can be said with reasonable confidence is narrow. Sweat is thermoregulation, not elimination. It does not clean pores, because it does not travel through them. Exercise is good for skin across years, mostly through circulation, sleep and stress rather than through anything that happens in the session. Most post-gym trouble is mechanical and logistical — friction, occlusion, sweat left to dry — rather than caused by sweat. What cannot be said is how much, how quickly, or for whom. Anyone offering a number there has invented it.

We have six formulations in development at our laboratory in Barcelona and none of them on sale, which makes this an unusually easy piece to write honestly, because there is nothing at the end of it to buy. The most useful object in this article is a sink.
